candidateAssessment.concept: Comparative biology, animal health and disease science
candidateAssessment.assessment: Comparative neurobiology and biodiversity, anatomy, human physiology, disease mechanisms, infection and pharmacology provide meaningful foundations. The courses lack a comparative sequence in the organ systems, reproduction, feeding and diseases of relevant animal species.

candidateAssessment.concept: One Health, disease ecology and welfare
candidateAssessment.assessment: Epidemiology and infection, comparative neurobiology, husbandry and aquaculture, ecology and environmental governance provide genuine overlap. The plan lacks sustained zoonosis control, veterinary public health, and practical animal welfare assessment within a study of animal disease.

candidateAssessment.concept: Veterinary diagnosis and clinical animal care
candidateAssessment.assessment: Anatomical observation, microbial laboratory work, human disease mechanisms and research-based health psychology provide transferable skills. Clinical animal examination, diagnostic reasoning across species, anaesthesia and surgical skills have no connected taught sequence.

findings: The initial comparison passed feasibility. The first test replaces a general mathematics course with Functional Anatomy, making the strongest biological route more directly responsive. It retains laboratory microbiology, blood and tissue study, biochemistry, physiology, pathology, immunology, pharmacology, ecology and comparative neurobiology. Human systems and diseases dominate the organ courses. Neurobiology provides genuinely comparative nervous-system anatomy, animal behaviour, welfare and research ethics, but cannot supply multispecies organ-system anatomy, physiology and pathology. The second test deliberately concentrates on One Health and keeps epidemiology, infection, ecology, husbandry, aquaculture and environmental policy. It covers population risk, ecosystems and farming pressures, but lacks a sustained study of zoonotic transmission and control, veterinary food and public health, and direct assessment of animal welfare. The third test strengthens the potential clinical response with anatomy and human consultation and symptom reasoning. It does not provide supervised clinical examination of animals, differential diagnoses by species, anaesthesia or surgical techniques. Candidate differences are sensitivity tests and do not establish viable programme alternatives. Description-only contributions were assessed from their actual content. The finding rests on the academic scope, with all three test schedules feasible.
